annotations.source_pub: Plutarch's Lives, tr. Aubrey Stewart & George Long, vol. 4 (London, 1892 printing) (PD)
annotations.quote:
During the campaign all the daytime when he was not with Pompeius he was
employed about study and books; and not only at other times, but also
before the great battle. It was the height of summer, and the heat was
excessive, as they were encamped close to marshy ground; and those who
carried the tent of Brutus did not come quickly. After being much
harassed about these matters, and having scarcely by midday anointed
himself and taken a little to eat, while the rest were either sleeping
or engaged in thought and care about the future, he kept on writing till
evening-time, making an epitome of Polybius.
annotations.note: On the eve of Pharsalus in 48 BC, with the Republic's fate about to be settled, the man who would help kill Caesar less than four years later spent a sweltering afternoon abridging Polybius. Plutarch tells it as a portrait of the scholar-soldier, but beside this chapter it reads as something sharper: a Roman in the middle of a civil war, reaching for the book that explained how Rome came to rule the world, and taking literally the claim Polybius opens with, that the memory of others' reversals is the only teacher of how to bear the changes of fortune. The epitome itself is lost.

annotations.source_pub: Cicero, De Officiis, tr. Walter Miller (Loeb Classical Library, 1913) (PD)
annotations.quote:
Marcus Atilius Regulus in his second consulship was taken prisoner in
Africa by the stratagem of Xanthippus, a Spartan general serving under
the command of Hannibal's father Hamilcar. ... He was sent to the senate
on parole, sworn to return to Carthage himself ... And when his counsel
prevailed, the prisoners were retained and he himself returned to
Carthage; affection for his country and his family failed to hold him
back. And even then he was not ignorant of the fact that he was going to
a most cruel enemy and to exquisite torture; still, he thought his oath
must be sacredly kept.
annotations.note: Cicero's Regulus, who kept his oath all the way to torture and death, became Rome's favourite example of good faith. Polybius takes Regulus as far as a Carthaginian prison and then drops him; the lesson he draws (1.35) is about the danger of trusting Fortune in success and the power of one clear mind, Xanthippus', not about honour. The embassy, the oath and the return appear only in later Roman tradition, and Polybius' silence is the main reason many historians suspect the most famous part of the story is patriotic legend.

annotations.source_pub: The Federalist Papers (Project Gutenberg text of the 1787-88 essays) (PD)
annotations.quote:
The Achaean league, as it is called, was another society of Grecian
republics, which supplies us with valuable instruction. ... It appears
that the cities had all the same laws and customs, the same weights and
measures, and the same money. ... It is much to be regretted that such
imperfect monuments remain of this curious political fabric. Could its
interior structure and regular operation be ascertained, it is probable
that more light would be thrown by it on the science of federal
government, than by any of the like experiments with which we are
acquainted.
annotations.note: Writing as "Publius" in December 1787, Madison went looking for the best-organized confederacy in history and found the Achaean League, whose story survives chiefly because Polybius, the son of an Achaean general, told it. "The same weights and measures, and the same money" is Polybius' own detail from this chapter (2.37). Madison's regret over the "imperfect monuments" is partly a regret over this work's own losses: the later books that followed the League to its end survive only in fragments.

annotations.source_pub: The Spirit of Laws, tr. Thomas Nugent (New York: Colonial Press, 1899) (PD)
annotations.quote:
That judicious writer, Polybius, informs us that music was necessary to
soften the manners of the Arcadians, who lived in a cold, gloomy
country; that the inhabitants of Cynete, who slighted music, were the
cruellest of all the Greeks, and that no other town was so immersed in
luxury and debauchery.
annotations.note: Montesquieu opens his chapter on a "paradox of the ancients" with this digression: why did serious Greek lawgivers treat music as a matter of state? Polybius' answer (the last clause of the quotation, on luxury and debauchery, is Montesquieu's own gloss; Polybius calls the Cynaethans savage and impious, not luxurious), that the Arcadians made music compulsory up to the age of thirty to soften men hardened by a harsh land, and that Cynaetha, the one town that gave it up, became a byword for savagery, is exactly the kind of evidence Montesquieu wanted. His larger argument, that climate shapes character and laws must answer to both, has one of its ancient roots in these two chapters.

annotations.source_pub: The Republic of Cicero, tr. G. W. Featherstonhaugh (New York, 1829) (PD)
annotations.quote:
Thus do they snatch the government of the commonwealth from each other
like a ball—tyrants from kings—chiefs or the people from tyrants; and
factions or tyrants from them, nor does the same mode of government ever
last a long time. ... Nevertheless one which shall be well tempered and
balanced out of all those three kinds of government, is better than
that; yet there should be always something royal and pre-eminent in a
government, at the same time that some power should be placed in the
hands of the better class, and other things reserved for the judgment
and will of the multitude. ... This cannot well happen in such a
combined and moderately balanced government, unless by the great vices
of the chief persons.
annotations.note: Cicero set his dialogue in 129 BC and gave the leading part to Scipio Aemilianus, Polybius' friend and pupil, who later in the work calls him "our guest Polybius." The theory Scipio expounds here, with governments tossed from hand to hand "like a ball" and stability found only in a balance of king, nobles and people, is Book 6's, now spoken by the Roman Polybius knew best. The dialogue nearly shared Polybius' fate: lost for centuries, it was recovered from a Vatican palimpsest in 1819, and the gaps still show in this translation.

annotations.work: Discourses on the First Decade of Titus Livius, I.2
annotations.source_pub: Discourses on the First Decade of Titus Livius, tr. Ninian Hill Thomson (London, 1883) (PD)
annotations.quote:
Other, and, as many have thought, wiser teachers, will have it, that
there are altogether six forms of government, three of them utterly bad,
the other three good in themselves, but so readily corrupted that they
too are apt to become hurtful. ... For this is the circle revolving
within which all States are and have been governed ... Wise legislators
therefore, knowing these defects, and avoiding each of these forms in
its simplicity, have made choice of a form which shares in the qualities
of all the first three, and which they judge to be more stable and
lasting than any of these separately. For where we have a monarchy, an
aristocracy, and a democracy existing together in the same city, each of
the three serves as a check upon the other.
annotations.note: Machiavelli never names his source; the six forms and their cycle come from "other, and, as many have thought, wiser teachers." The teacher is Polybius, and the chapter follows his Book 6 argument step by step: the herd choosing the strongest, the birth of justice from anger at ingratitude, each good form sliding into its corrupt twin, and the escape into a mixed constitution on the model of Lycurgus. Machiavelli keeps Polybius' contrast between Sparta and Rome (6.10) but changes its terms: where Polybius has Rome learning through struggle and reverses, Machiavelli says she "obtained by chance" what her founders failed to provide, out of the quarrels of commons and senate.

annotations.work: A Defence of the Constitutions of Government of the United States of America, vol. I
annotations.source_pub: The Works of John Adams, ed. Charles Francis Adams, vol. 4 (Boston, 1851) (PD)
annotations.quote:
Thus, my dear sir, you see that Polybius's opinion of different orders,
checks, and balances, in a commonwealth, is very different from that of
M. Turgot. The Roman constitution formed the noblest people and the
greatest power that has ever existed. ... But if all the powers of the
consuls, senate, and people had been centred in a single assembly of the
people, collectively or representatively, will any man pretend to
believe that they would have been long free, or ever great? ... The
distribution of power was, however, never accurately or judiciously made
in that constitution. The executive was never sufficiently separated
from the legislative, nor had these powers a control upon each other
defined with sufficient accuracy. ... The constitutions of several of
the United States, it is hoped, will prove themselves improvements both
upon the Roman, the Spartan, and the English commonwealths.
annotations.note: Adams wrote the Defence in London to answer Turgot, who had criticized the new American states for copying England's balance of orders. After quoting this part of Book 6 at length, he enlists Polybius against Turgot and then argues back: Rome never properly separated executive from legislative, and Americans can do better. It is Polybius' checks and balances offered to American constitution-makers with amendments.

annotations.source_pub: Cicero, De Officiis, tr. Walter Miller (Loeb Classical Library, 1913) (PD)
annotations.quote:
Historians are not in agreement in regard to the facts. Polybius, one of
the very best authorities, states that of the ten eminent nobles who
were sent at that time, nine returned when their mission failed at the
hands of the senate. But one of the ten, who, a little while after
leaving the camp, had gone back on the pretext that he had forgotten
something or other, remained behind at Rome; he explained that by his
return to the camp he was released from the obligation of his oath. He
was wrong; for deceit does not remove the guilt of perjury--it merely
aggravates it. ... And so the senate ordered that the cunning scoundrel
should be taken back to Hannibal in chains.
annotations.note: Writing to his son in the autumn after Caesar's murder, Cicero names Polybius "one of the very best authorities" and retells this chapter almost point for point: the ten envoys, the one who turned back for something forgotten, the senate sending him back in chains, the eight thousand left unransomed. The difference is the moral. Polybius tells the story to show the strength of the Roman constitution; Cicero turns it into a lesson in ethics, and he prefers Polybius' version to a rival account in which several envoys played the same trick.

annotations.work: Excerpta Constantiniana, preface to "On Embassies of the Romans to Foreign Peoples"
annotations.source_pub: Translated for this edition (CC0) from the Greek text ed. C. de Boor, Excerpta historica iussu Imp. Constantini Porphyrogeniti confecta, vol. 1 (Berlin, 1903)
annotations.quote:
All those of old, kings and private men alike, who did not let pleasure
sweep their minds away or grow soft, but kept the nobility of their
souls unstained through virtue: these above all persevered in labour and gave
themselves to letters ... But since, in the course of so many years,
events multiplied beyond measure and writings were woven without end,
the web of history spread out into something boundless and
unmanageable; and since in later times men's inclinations were bound to
lean toward the worse, to grow careless of what is good and idle about
taking up the record of earlier ages ... so that the discovery of history
was overshadowed by obscurity, partly through a scarcity of useful
books, partly because people shrank in dread from sprawling
verbosity: Constantine, born in the purple, the most orthodox and most
Christian of all who have ever reigned, keener-eyed in
discerning what is good and possessed of an active mind, judged it best,
of common benefit and profitable for life, first to gather by diligent
search books from every quarter of the inhabited world, pregnant with
knowledge of every sort; and then, since the sheer bulk of their
prolixity wears out the ear and seems, besides, to most people tiresome and
burdensome, he thought it necessary to cut this up into small portions,
and to set out ungrudgingly, for all to share, the benefit that springs
from them ... and to divide it into distinct subjects, fifty-three in
number, in which and under which every great deed of history is
enclosed. ... They are taken from the chronicles listed below: 1. Peter
the Patrician and Magister. 2. The Chronicle of George the Monk. 3. John
of Antioch. 4. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities. 5.
Polybius of Megalopolis.
annotations.note: The emperor whose scissors saved this book. Around 950 Constantine VII had the Greek histories in his library cut up and filed under fifty-three subjects; most of the subjects are lost, but those that survive, above all "On Embassies," "On Virtues and Vices" and "On Sentences," are where much of what we have of Books 7 to 40 comes from. Much of what follows survives because of the editorial decision this preface defends. Note the fourth and fifth names on his list: Dionysius, who complained that no one could finish Polybius, filed beside the historian he disparaged.

annotations.work: Preface to the Extract from the Commentaries of the Chevalier Folard on the History of Polybius
annotations.source_pub: Translated for this edition (CC0) from the French text in Oeuvres de Frédéric le Grand, ed. J. D. E. Preuss, Oeuvres militaires, vol. 1 (Berlin, 1856)
annotations.quote:
The work we present to you may be called the Spirit of M. de Folard.
Among the visions and extravagances of this illustrious soldier there
are treasures: he had buried diamonds in the middle of a dunghill, and we
have dug them out, and instead of six fat quarto volumes we give
enthusiasts a quarter of one of them. We have made short work of the
system of columns ... Among the great number of books that are written,
very few are pure gold; there are even few from which one could draw as
many good things as from the Commentary on Polybius. For the progress of
human knowledge it would be desirable that, rather than writing new
books, people applied themselves to making good extracts of those we
already have; one might then hope not to waste one's time in reading.
... The art of war, which surely deserves to be studied and mastered as
much as any of the other arts, still lacks classic books. We have few.
Caesar, in his Commentaries, teaches us hardly anything beyond what we
see in the war of the Pandours ... a general of our day could make use
of nothing but the disposition of his cavalry at the battle of
Pharsalus. ... Those who have had this abridgment printed have had no
aim but the greater glory of the service, in trying to make it easier
for officers to study the study of their art and of a profession that leads to
immortality.
annotations.note: Polybius argues in these chapters that command is an art to be learned from study as well as from the camp. In 1753 Frederick the Great took him at his word, having Folard's six-volume commentary on Polybius cut down to a quarter of one volume and printed in just 110 copies for his officers, with Folard's pet theory of attack in deep columns thrown out and the "diamonds" kept. Like Constantine eight centuries earlier, a monarch decided that the way to make a long book useful was to cut it. From all of Caesar, the one thing he thinks a modern general can use is the placing of the cavalry at Pharsalus, the battle on whose eve Brutus sat making his own epitome of Polybius.

annotations.work: Considerations on the Causes of the Grandeur of the Romans, ch. V
annotations.source_pub: Montesquieu's Considerations on the Causes of the Grandeur and Decadence of the Romans, tr. Jehu Baker (New York, 1882) (PD)
annotations.quote:
With his usual good sense, Polybius compares the military method of the
Romans with that of the Macedonians—which last had been adopted by all
the successors of Alexander the Great. He points out the advantages and
the inconveniences of the phalanx and the legion. He gives the
preference to the latter; and, if we are to judge by the events of the
time, it would appear that he was right.
annotations.note: Montesquieu's short book on why Rome rose and fell leans on Polybius throughout, and at Cynoscephalae it simply defers to him: the legion beat the phalanx because it could fight on any ground, while the phalanx needed a battlefield made for it. The translator's note in this edition shows that Bossuet had already endorsed the same verdict. Polybius' comparison in these chapters became the starting point of the eighteenth-century argument over column and line that Folard and Frederick the Great carried on.

annotations.source_pub: Dionysius of Halicarnassus On Literary Composition, tr. W. Rhys Roberts (London: Macmillan, 1910) (PD)
annotations.quote:
At last, in later times, it was utterly neglected; no one thought it
absolutely indispensable, or that it contributed anything to the beauty
of discourse. Consequently they left behind them lucubrations that no
one has the patience to read from beginning to end. I mean men like
Phylarchus, Duris, Polybius, Psaon, Demetrius of Callatis, Hieronymus,
Antigonus, Heracleides, Hegesianax, and countless others: a whole day
would not be enough if I tried to repeat the bare names of them all!
annotations.note: If you are reading this note at the last chapter, you have just refuted it. Dionysius, a Greek critic teaching in Augustan Rome, cared about the music of word order, and Polybius' plain, workmanlike prose struck him as tone-deaf; he files the greatest historian of the age between Duris and Psaon, whom almost nobody now reads. Posterity has been kinder to the history than Dionysius was to the prose, though only five of the forty books survive whole.
